introduction.p: Derivative calculations must respect the model's domain and constraints. A critical point may be infeasible or only a local optimum, and Newton's method may fail to converge. These examples show how to check those possibilities.

subsection.title: A critical point outside the physical domain
subsection.p: where q is the number of units produced.
If all production levels were allowed, the maximum would occur at q=40, because P is a downward-opening parabola.
But suppose a contract requires the company to produce between 50 and 100 units:
Then the critical point q=40 is outside the physical domain.
So P is decreasing throughout the allowed interval. The maximum allowed profit occurs at the left endpoint:

figure.caption: The critical point q=40 maximizes the formula on a larger domain, but it is not an allowed production level.

description.p: The critical point q=40 maximizes the formula on a larger domain, but it is not an allowed production level.

note.title: Moral
note.p: A critical point outside the physical domain is not a possible answer. The domain is part of the model.

exercise.title: Why can a critical point outside the physical domain be irrelevant?

statement.p: A derivative can locate the vertex of a profit parabola even when a contract forbids that production level. In your own words, why is that not a failure of calculus, and why must the allowed interval be part of the question before a critical number is trusted?

hint.p: A calculus method is only as good as the question it is applied to. The derivative answers the model we wrote, including a domain we may have forgotten.

subsection.title: A local maximum that is not the absolute maximum
subsection.p: A local maximum is a high point nearby. An absolute maximum is a high point everywhere in the domain.
The derivative is positive on (-\infty,-1), negative on (-1,1), and positive on (1,\infty). Therefore x=-1 is a local maximum, and x=1 is a local minimum.

description.p: A local high point can lose to an endpoint or to another part of the graph.

note.title: Moral
note.p: A local maximum is not automatically an absolute maximum. For absolute extrema on a closed interval, check all candidates: interior critical points and endpoints.

exercise.title: Why can a local maximum fail to be the absolute maximum?

statement.p: A nearby peak can lose to an endpoint or to a better peak farther away. In your own words, why does finding f'(x)=0 not finish an applied optimization problem, and what extra comparisons turn a local candidate into a global decision?

hint.p: Check endpoints, check the physical domain, and ask whether the result is local or absolute. A first-derivative test is a neighborhood test.

subsection.title: Newton’s method can find the wrong root
subsection.p: Newton’s method follows tangent lines. A tangent line can cross the x-axis far from the root we had in mind.
Suppose we want to find the positive root 2, and we start with
The method lands exactly on the root
That is a root of the equation, but not the root we intended to find.

figure.caption: The tangent line at x_0=1 crosses the axis at the root -2, not at the intended root 2.

description.p: The tangent line at x_0=1 crosses the axis at the root -2, not at the intended root 2.

note.title: Moral
note.p: Newton’s method is local. A starting point that seems reasonable may still lead to a different root.

subsection.p: Bracketing can help. If the goal is the root 2, we can first isolate it by checking signs on an interval such as
Then we can monitor whether Newton’s iterates remain near the intended interval.

exercise.title: Why can Newton’s method find the wrong root, or fail to converge?

statement.p: A tangent from a bad starting guess can leap to a different root, cycle, or hit a horizontal tangent. In your own words, why is fast local behavior compatible with global unreliability, and what should we check before trusting the iterates?

hint.p: Newton’s method needs a good starting point and a nonzero derivative. Ask whether the iterates stabilize and whether f(x_n) is actually small.

subsection.title: Newton’s method may not converge
subsection.p: Sometimes Newton’s method does not merely find the wrong root. Sometimes it does not settle down at all.
The function does have a real root. For example,
By the Intermediate Value Theorem, a root lies between -2 and -1. Newton’s method did not fail because no root exists. It failed because the starting point made the tangent process cycle.

note.title: Moral
note.p: Newton’s method needs a good starting point and a nonzero derivative. It is fast when it behaves well, but it is not guaranteed to behave well from every starting point.

subsection.title: The common lesson
subsection.p: The warning examples have one message:

p.me: \text{A calculus method is only as good as the question it is applied to.}

exercise.title: Why is a calculus method only as good as the question it is applied to?

statement.p: The warning examples of this section have one common lesson. In your own words, why do domain, endpoints, local-versus-absolute, units, and starting guesses all belong inside the mathematics rather than after it?

hint.p: A derivative answers the question asked by the model. If the model has the wrong domain or the wrong interpretation, the derivative may still compute something, just not the thing we needed.
